about: Short passages the site may quote, word for word: Plato in Benjamin Jowett's public-domain English translation, and Aristotle, Plato's student, in W. D. Ross's. Ask Socrates (/socrates) may quote only from this file, and the pages' epigraphs are rendered from it. Each text was cut from the source named in source_text_url and is checked against it by scripts/verify_passages.py (whitespace collapsed and curly quotes counted as straight, otherwise exact); Ross's passages are also checked word for word against the scan of the printed Oxford edition (print_url). The file keeps its old name so that everything that reads it keeps working.

translations.Aristotle, Metaphysics: W. D. Ross, Metaphysica, 2nd edition (Oxford, 1928), public domain in the US
translations.Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics: W. D. Ross, Ethica Nicomachea (Oxford, 1925), public domain in the US

license: Public domain. Jowett's translation (1892): Project Gutenberg texts are free of copyright in the United States; this file carries only short excerpts, without Gutenberg's header or trademark. Ross's translations of the Metaphysics (2nd edition, Oxford, 1928) and the Nicomachean Ethics (Oxford, 1925) were published more than 95 years ago, so they are in the public domain in the United States (in the UK and the EU they stay in copyright until the end of 2041, 70 years after Ross's death). Short excerpts only. The digital text checked against is the MIT Internet Classics Archive's (classics.mit.edu); the printed editions are the Internet Archive's scans.
stephanus_note: Gutenberg's Jowett texts have no Stephanus numbers. Each reference gives the page and section of the standard Stephanus pagination, placed by matching the passage with editions that print it (Perseus Digital Library); spot-checked for Republic 598a and 515b, Cratylus 427b and Phaedrus 275d and 276a. Aristotle's passages carry Bekker numbers (page, column and line), read from the margins of the printed Oxford editions, which number every fifth line.
attribution: Aristotle was Plato's student, as Plato was Socrates'. Quote an Aristotle passage as Aristotle's (Socrates may call him his student's student), never as Plato's or Socrates' own words.

verified.method: exact substring of the source text (whitespace collapsed, curly quotes as straight); Aristotle also word for word in the printed edition's scan

not_included.what: Aristotle, Physics II.3, 194b17-20, the four causes (R. P. Hardie and R. K. Gaye, Oxford, 1930)
not_included.why: Public domain in the US only since 1 January 2026, and the only clean digital text (MIT) drops a word in this very passage ('the why of (which' where the 1930 printing has 'the why of it (which'), so it can't be checked verbatim against a clean text. Metaphysics V.2 (1013a24-33), which repeats the four causes almost word for word, is used instead.

not_included.what: Apology 38a as 'the life which is unexamined is not worth living'
not_included.why: Not the wording of Jowett's text on Project Gutenberg, which reads 'the unexamined life is not worth living'; that wording is used.

not_included.what: Aristotle in Ross's 1908 first edition of the Metaphysics
not_included.why: The only clean digital text (MIT) is Ross's revised 2nd edition of 1928 (it reads 'the several memories' and 'definition' where 1908 has 'many memories' and 'formula'), so the 1928 edition is the one quoted and checked. It is equally in the US public domain.

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates, to Glaucon
passages.title: One Form for each common name
passages.text: Whenever a number of individuals have a common name, we assume them to have also a corresponding idea or form:—do you understand me?

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates and Glaucon
passages.title: Many beds, one Form; the maker looks to the idea
passages.text: Let us take any common instance; there are beds and tables in the world—plenty of them, are there not? Yes. But there are only two ideas or forms of them—one the idea of a bed, the other of a table. True. And the maker of either of them makes a bed or he makes a table for our use, in accordance with the idea—that is our way of speaking in this and similar instances—but no artificer makes the ideas themselves: how could he?

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates and Glaucon
passages.title: The painter, a creator of appearances
passages.text: And the painter too is, as I conceive, just such another—a creator of appearances, is he not?

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates and Glaucon
passages.title: Three beds: God's, the carpenter's, the painter's
passages.text: Well then, here are three beds: one existing in nature, which is made by God, as I think that we may say—for no one else can be the maker? No. There is another which is the work of the carpenter? Yes. And the work of the painter is a third? Yes. Beds, then, are of three kinds, and there are three artists who superintend them: God, the maker of the bed, and the painter?

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates and Glaucon
passages.title: Only one ideal bed
passages.text: God, whether from choice or from necessity, made one bed in nature and one only; two or more such ideal beds neither ever have been nor ever will be made by God. Why is that? Because even if He had made but two, a third would still appear behind them which both of them would have for their idea, and that would be the ideal bed and not the two others.

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates and Glaucon
passages.title: A bed seen from different points of view
passages.text: I mean, that you may look at a bed from different points of view, obliquely or directly or from any other point of view, and the bed will appear different, but there is no difference in reality. And the same of all things. Yes, he said, the difference is only apparent.

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates and Glaucon
passages.title: Painting imitates appearance, far from the truth
passages.text: Which is the art of painting designed to be—an imitation of things as they are, or as they appear—of appearance or of reality? Of appearance. Then the imitator, I said, is a long way off the truth, and can do all things because he lightly touches on a small part of them, and that part an image.

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates
passages.title: The Cave
passages.text: And now, I said, let me show in a figure how far our nature is enlightened or unenlightened:—Behold! human beings living in a underground den, which has a mouth open towards the light and reaching all along the den; here they have been from their childhood, and have their legs and necks chained so that they cannot move, and can only see before them, being prevented by the chains from turning round their heads.

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates, to Glaucon
passages.title: The prisoners name the shadows
passages.text: And if they were able to converse with one another, would they not suppose that they were naming what was actually before them?

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates and Glaucon
passages.title: Truth as nothing but shadows
passages.text: To them, I said, the truth would be literally nothing but the shadows of the images. That is certain.

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Hermogenes, reporting Cratylus
passages.title: Names are natural, not conventional (Cratylus' view)
passages.text: I should explain to you, Socrates, that our friend Cratylus has been arguing about names; he says that they are natural and not conventional; not a portion of the human voice which men agree to use; but that there is a truth or correctness in them, which is the same for Hellenes as for barbarians.

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Hermogenes
passages.title: Names are convention and agreement (Hermogenes' view)
passages.text: I have often talked over this matter, both with Cratylus and others, and cannot convince myself that there is any principle of correctness in names other than convention and agreement; any name which you give, in my opinion, is the right one, and if you change that and give another, the new name is as correct as the old

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates
passages.title: Lambda, the sound of smoothness
passages.text: he further observed the liquid movement of lambda, in the pronunciation of which the tongue slips, and in this he found the expression of smoothness

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: King Thamus, in Socrates' story
passages.title: The semblance of truth, the show of wisdom
passages.text: you give your disciples not truth, but only the semblance of truth; they will be hearers of many things and will have learned nothing; they will appear to be omniscient and will generally know nothing; they will be tiresome company, having the show of wisdom without the reality.

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates
passages.title: Written words give one unvarying answer
passages.text: I cannot help feeling, Phaedrus, that writing is unfortunately like painting; for the creations of the painter have the attitude of life, and yet if you ask them a question they preserve a solemn silence. And the same may be said of speeches. You would imagine that they had intelligence, but if you want to know anything and put a question to one of them, the speaker always gives one unvarying answer.

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Phaedrus, to Socrates, who agrees
passages.title: The living word, and the written word its image
passages.text: You mean the living word of knowledge which has a soul, and of which the written word is properly no more than an image?

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates
passages.title: All learning is recollection
passages.text: for as all nature is akin, and the soul has learned all things; there is no difficulty in her eliciting or as men say learning, out of a single recollection all the rest, if a man is strenuous and does not faint; for all enquiry and all learning is but recollection.

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates, to Theaetetus
passages.title: Philosophy begins in wonder
passages.text: I see, my dear Theaetetus, that Theodorus had a true insight into your nature when he said that you were a philosopher, for wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates, at his trial
passages.title: The unexamined life is not worth living
passages.text: daily to discourse about virtue, and of those other things about which you hear me examining myself and others, is the greatest good of man, and that the unexamined life is not worth living

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Timaeus
passages.title: Everything that becomes has a cause
passages.text: Now everything that becomes or is created must of necessity be created by some cause, for without a cause nothing can be created.

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates, to Glaucon
passages.title: Knowledge is not put in, like sight into blind eyes
passages.text: But then, if I am right, certain professors of education must be wrong when they say that they can put a knowledge into the soul which was not there before, like sight into blind eyes.

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates, to Glaucon
passages.title: Education turns an eye that already sees
passages.text: And must there not be some art which will effect conversion in the easiest and quickest manner; not implanting the faculty of sight, for that exists already, but has been turned in the wrong direction, and is looking away from the truth?

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates, to Glaucon
passages.title: Third in descent from nature: the imitator
passages.text: Good, I said; then you call him who is third in the descent from nature an imitator?

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates, to Meno
passages.title: Asked the same questions in different forms
passages.text: And at present these notions have just been stirred up in him, as in a dream; but if he were frequently asked the same questions, in different forms, he would know as well as any one at last?

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates, to Meno
passages.title: We are better for enquiring
passages.text: we shall be better and braver and less helpless if we think that we ought to enquire, than we should have been if we indulged in the idle fancy that there was no knowing and no use in seeking to know what we do not know

passages.author: Plato
passages.speaker: Socrates, to Cratylus
passages.title: Learn from the things, not from their names
passages.text: How real existence is to be studied or discovered is, I suspect, beyond you and me. But we may admit so much, that the knowledge of things is not to be derived from names. No; they must be studied and investigated in themselves.

passages.author: Aristotle
passages.speaker: Aristotle
passages.title: All men by nature desire to know
passages.text: All men by nature desire to know. An indication of this is the delight we take in our senses; for even apart from their usefulness they are loved for themselves; and above all others the sense of sight.
passages.as_printed: ALL men by nature desire to know. An indication of this is the delight we take in our senses; for even apart from their usefulness they are loved for themselves; and above all others the sense of sight.
passages.translation: W. D. Ross, Metaphysica, 2nd edition (Oxford, 1928), public domain in the US

passages.author: Aristotle
passages.speaker: Aristotle
passages.title: From many experiences, one universal judgement
passages.text: Now art arises when from many notions gained by experience one universal judgement about a class of objects is produced.
passages.translation: W. D. Ross, Metaphysica, 2nd edition (Oxford, 1928), public domain in the US

passages.author: Aristotle
passages.speaker: Aristotle
passages.title: Knowing that, and knowing why
passages.text: For men of experience know that the thing is so, but do not know why, while the others know the ‘why’ and the cause.
passages.translation: W. D. Ross, Metaphysica, 2nd edition (Oxford, 1928), public domain in the US

passages.author: Aristotle
passages.speaker: Aristotle
passages.title: Can the Forms exist apart from the things?
passages.text: Again, it would seem impossible that the substance and that of which it is the substance should exist apart; how, therefore, could the Ideas, being the substances of things, exist apart?
passages.translation: W. D. Ross, Metaphysica, 2nd edition (Oxford, 1928), public domain in the US

passages.author: Aristotle
passages.speaker: Aristotle
passages.title: The four causes
passages.text: ‘Cause’ means (1) that from which, as immanent material, a thing comes into being, e.g. the bronze is the cause of the statue and the silver of the saucer, and so are the classes which include these. (2) The form or pattern, i.e. the definition of the essence, and the classes which include this (e.g. the ratio 2:1 and number in general are causes of the octave), and the parts included in the definition. (3) That from which the change or the resting from change first begins; e.g. the adviser is a cause of the action, and the father a cause of the child, and in general the maker a cause of the thing made and the change-producing of the changing. (4) The end, i.e. that for the sake of which a thing is; e.g. health is the cause of walking.
passages.translation: W. D. Ross, Metaphysica, 2nd edition (Oxford, 1928), public domain in the US

passages.author: Aristotle
passages.speaker: Aristotle
passages.title: Truth above friends (on Plato's Forms)
passages.text: Yet it would perhaps be thought to be better, indeed to be our duty, for the sake of maintaining the truth even to destroy what touches us closely, especially as we are philosophers or lovers of wisdom; for, while both are dear, piety requires us to honour truth above our friends.
passages.translation: W. D. Ross, Ethica Nicomachea (Oxford, 1925), public domain in the US

passages.author: Aristotle
passages.speaker: Aristotle
passages.title: We learn by doing
passages.text: For the things we have to learn before we can do them, we learn by doing them, e.g. men become builders by building
passages.translation: W. D. Ross, Ethica Nicomachea (Oxford, 1925), public domain in the US
